103	\section{VOTA Extraction Algorithm}
104	\label{sec:vota_algorithm}
105	
106	Algorithm~\ref{alg:vota} describes the three-component VOTA extraction pipeline applied to a raw \texttt{sys.settrace} execution log.
107	
108	\begin{algorithm}[t]
109	\caption{VOTA Trace Extraction}
110	\label{alg:vota}
111	\small
112	\begin{algorithmic}[1]
113	\REQUIRE Raw trace $T$ from \texttt{sys.settrace} (list of events)
114	\ENSURE Compressed VOTA representation $V$
115	\STATE $V \leftarrow$ empty string
116	\STATE \textbf{// Component 1: Exception summary}
117	\FOR{each event $e$ in $T$ with type \texttt{exception}}
118	  \STATE Parse traceback $\rightarrow$ extract error type, message, file, line
119	  \STATE Append \texttt{[ERROR] type: message (file:line)} to $V$
120	\ENDFOR
121	\IF{no exception events found}
122	  \STATE Append \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} to $V$
123	\ENDIF
124	\STATE \textbf{// Component 2: Assertion-point comparison}
125	\FOR{each \texttt{assert} or \texttt{return} event $e$ in $T$}
126	  \STATE Extract actual value from execution state
127	  \STATE Extract expected value from test assertion
128	  \STATE Append \texttt{[ASSERT] actual=... expected=... match=T/F} to $V$
129	\ENDFOR
130	\STATE \textbf{// Component 3: Loop compression}
131	\FOR{each consecutive repeated line sequence $S$ in $T$}
132	  \IF{$|S| \geq 2$ iterations of same loop body}
133	    \STATE Replace $S$ with single iteration + \texttt{[repeated $\times$N]}
134	  \ENDIF
135	\ENDFOR
136	\STATE Append compressed non-exception lines to $V$
137	\RETURN $V$
138	\end{algorithmic}
139	\end{algorithm}

142	\section{VOTA Trace Examples}
143	\label{sec:vota_examples}
144	
145	We provide two representative VOTA trace examples illustrating the fail and pass cases.
146	In the fail case, the exception event provides an unambiguous fault signal.
147	In the pass case, the absence of an exception event combined with a matching assertion point confirms correct execution.
148	
149	\paragraph{Fail example.}
150	A \texttt{ZeroDivisionError} triggers an \texttt{[ERROR]} event, providing a direct fault signal that is sufficient for the model to predict \texttt{fail}.
151	
152	\begin{scriptsize}
153	\begin{verbatim}
154	## Function
155	def divide(a, b):
156	    return a / b
157	
158	## Test Input
159	divide(1, 0)
160	
161	## Expected Output
162	inf
163	
164	## VOTA Trace
165	[ERROR] ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
166	
167	## Verdict
168	fail
169	\end{verbatim}
170	\end{scriptsize}
171	
172	\paragraph{Pass example.}
173	No exception is raised, and the assertion point confirms that the actual output matches the expected value.
174	
175	\begin{scriptsize}
176	\begin{verbatim}
177	## Function
178	def add(a, b):
179	    return a + b
180	
181	## Test Input
182	add(2, 3)
183	
184	## Expected Output
185	5
186	
187	## VOTA Trace
188	[LOOP] No loops detected.
189	[ASSERT] actual=5, expected=5
190	
191	## Verdict
192	pass

194	\end{scriptsize}

197	This binary signal (presence vs.\ absence of an exception) is sufficient for near-perfect verdict prediction.

253	\section{Tokenizer and Truncation Analysis}
254	\label{sec:tokenizer_analysis}
255	
256	DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure driven by tokenizer-induced truncation.
257	Re-evaluation of the seed 42 checkpoint with the standard max\_length=2048 yields 16\% accuracy, confirming complete model collapse rather than marginal degradation.
258	The previously reported 84.45\% was obtained with max\_length=16384, which partially bypasses tokenizer truncation.
259	Seeds 123 and 456, evaluated under identical conditions, achieve 99.16\% and 99.33\% respectively.
260	The DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}929 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
261	The training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates trace content, so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the majority of samples.
262	Seeds 123 and 456 (99.16\% and 99.33\%) demonstrate that DeepSeek can learn VOTA when LoRA initialization avoids the truncation-sensitive basin; the 2-seed mean (99.25\%$\pm$0.12) matches the cross-model VOTA range (98.74--99.54\%).
263	
264	A post-hoc group analysis on seed 42 provides directional evidence: partitioning test samples by whether their training-set counterparts exceeded the context window, intact samples ($N{=}99$) achieve 100\% accuracy while truncated samples ($N{=}1{,}091$) achieve 83.04\% (95\% CI [80.75\%, 85.24\%]; Fisher exact $p{<}.001$), with all 185 errors concentrated in the fail class (fail recall = 31.23\%).
265	Per-class analysis (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) confirms that seed 42 achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}.
266	
267	Seed robustness is consistent across models: Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} produces identical 99.83\% across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}0$), and DeepSeek achieves 99.39\%$\pm$0.10 (seeds 42/456: 99.33\%, seed 123: 99.50\%).
268	Because \texttt{exception\_only} test inputs contain 48.99\% duplicates (607 unique of 1,190; \S\ref{sec:dataset}), CIs assume $n{=}1{,}190$ independent trials; under deduplication ($n{=}607$), Qwen's accuracy is 99.67\% (Wilson CI [98.81, 99.91]).

271	\section{Persistent Error Analysis}
272	\label{sec:irreducible}
273	
274	The \texttt{exception\_only} condition with Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B misclassifies exactly 2 out of 1,190 test samples across all three seeds (42, 123, 456), with 100\% overlap across seeds.
275	Both samples (IDs 901 and 905) share the following characteristics:
276	
277	\begin{itemize}
278	\item \textbf{Function:} \texttt{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95), a function that checks whether all dictionary keys are uniformly upper-case or lower-case strings.
279	\item \textbf{Ground-truth label:} \texttt{pass}.
280	\item \textbf{Predicted label:} \texttt{fail} (false negative).
281	\item \textbf{Cross-seed consistency:} Both samples are misclassified identically by all three seeds, indicating a systematic rather than stochastic error.
282	\end{itemize}
283	
284	Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \texttt{check\_dict\_case} uses \texttt{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \texttt{all()} short-circuits on the first \texttt{True} value, raising \texttt{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
285	Because \texttt{GeneratorExit} is a \texttt{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \texttt{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines, even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
286	The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
287	This is not a model failure but a representation ambiguity: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.
288	
289	Most configurations converge to these same 2 errors: Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-7B (3 seeds), CodeLlama-13B (seeds 42/456), and DeepSeek-6.7B (seeds 42/456) all produce error set $\{901, 905\}$.
290	However, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% accuracy (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.
291	This demonstrates that 99.83\% is a near-perfect \emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most LoRA initializations) rather than a hard data ceiling: the representation supports perfect accuracy, but most initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.
292	The practical implication is that these errors are high-probability convergence artifacts addressable through seed selection or ensemble methods, not fundamental limitations of the exception-based representation.

399	\paragraph{Non-monotonic pattern (head-truncation).}

400	Under head-truncation (retaining trace prefixes), the trend is non-monotonic: 512 tokens (80.42\%) slightly outperforms 256 tokens (78.82\%), but doubling to 1024 tokens \emph{decreases} accuracy to 77.23\%, a statistically significant 3.19pp drop ($p{=}.002$, 95\% CI [$-$5.29, $-$1.09]).
401	The no-limit condition (81.76\%) recovers and significantly exceeds 1024 tokens ($p{<}.001$), but 1024 tokens is not significantly better than \texttt{no\_trace} (75.13\%; $\Delta{=}{+}2.10$pp, $p{=}.078$, 95\% CI [$-$0.17, $+$4.37]).
402	This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation: the 1024-token prefix retains enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events that appear near the trace terminus.
403	Under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for Qwen-7B and Qwen-1.5B (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}); only DeepSeek-6.7B shows a mild $-$1.5pp decrease at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048, attributable to architecture-specific long-context sensitivity rather than a systematic mid-length pathology.
404	
405	\paragraph{Comparison to baselines.}
406	All four trace budget conditions significantly exceed \texttt{no\_trace} except 1024 tokens ($p{=}.078$), confirming that raw trace content provides some signal but unreliably so.
407	The gap to \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) is massive for every budget condition (18--23pp, all $p{<}.001$), underscoring that even unlimited raw traces cannot substitute for targeted signal extraction.
408	The best full-trace condition (no\_limit, 81.76\%) still lags \texttt{exception\_only} by 18.07pp (95\% CI [$-$20.34, $-$15.88]).
409	
410	\paragraph{Interpretation.}
411	These results rule out input truncation as the primary explanation for the full-trace performance gap: even with unlimited tokens, the model cannot extract the diagnostic signal that VOTA's targeted compression provides.
412	The non-monotonic dip at 1024 tokens is consistent with a ``worst-of-both-worlds'' regime where the model receives enough noisy context to dilute the signal but not enough to compensate through broader coverage.
413	The result reinforces the information density interpretation (\S\ref{sec:density}): the gap between full traces and VOTA is driven by the \emph{content} of the trace (irrelevant lines diluting the diagnostic signal), not its \emph{length}.
414	In contrast, VOTA's compressed representation concentrates the diagnostic signal into fewer tokens, making it sensitive to truncation when those tokens are removed (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).
415	
416	\paragraph{Truncation direction.}
417	Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: \texttt{tail\_2048} achieves 97.31\% vs.\ \texttt{head\_2048} (no\_limit) at 81.76\%, a 15.55pp improvement.
418	Even \texttt{tail\_512} (93.61\%) exceeds every head-truncation condition by over 11pp.
419	
420	However, \texttt{tail\_256} (77.48\%) performs at the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline level (75.13\%), indicating that the diagnostic signal does not reside in the very last trace lines.
421	The critical jump occurs between 256 and 512 tail tokens (+16.13pp), localizing the signal window to approximately 256--512 tokens from the trace terminus.
422	This is consistent with the trace format: the globals module dump consumes the first ${\sim}$384 tail tokens (pure noise), so structured execution markers (\texttt{[Line~X]} variable values) only become visible when the budget exceeds this threshold.

424	The 18.07pp gap from \texttt{full\_trace} to \texttt{exception\_only} decomposes as: 86\% positional concentration (recovered by tail-truncation at 2048 tokens) and 14\% residual content noise (the 2.52pp gap from \texttt{tail\_2048} to \texttt{exception\_only} that persists regardless of truncation direction).

634	\label{sec:robustness_analysis}
635	
636	The cross-model gap pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a design principle: \emph{trace representations should match the model capability floor, not the ceiling.}
637	Exception events are consistently the most effective component on both models, and their structural simplicity (a fixed-format error message) ensures that the relative advantage over richer representations holds across all seeds.
638	All three DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} seeds achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen and CodeLlama at ${\geq}$99.83\%.

641	Our \texttt{exception\_only} design sidesteps the truncation confound entirely: inputs have a median of 150 tokens (mean 398), well below the 2{,}048-token context window, so no training samples are truncated on either model.
642	The resulting 0.50pp cross-model gap (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) is therefore a clean measure of model capability differences, making the ``capability floor'' principle directly testable.
643	The practical implication is that trace-based systems should default to the simplest sufficient signal.

\section{VOTA Extraction Algorithm}
\label{sec:vota_algorithm}

Algorithm~\ref{alg:vota} describes the three-component VOTA extraction pipeline applied to a raw \texttt{sys.settrace} execution log.

\begin{algorithm}[t]
\caption{VOTA Trace Extraction}
\label{alg:vota}
\small
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
\REQUIRE Raw trace $T$ from \texttt{sys.settrace} (list of events)
\ENSURE Compressed VOTA representation $V$
\STATE $V \leftarrow$ empty string
\STATE \textbf{// Component 1: Exception summary}
\FOR{each event $e$ in $T$ with type \texttt{exception}}
  \STATE Parse traceback $\rightarrow$ extract error type, message, file, line
  \STATE Append \texttt{[ERROR] type: message (file:line)} to $V$
\ENDFOR
\IF{no exception events found}
  \STATE Append \texttt{[No exception data in trace]} to $V$
\ENDIF
\STATE \textbf{// Component 2: Assertion-point comparison}
\FOR{each \texttt{assert} or \texttt{return} event $e$ in $T$}
  \STATE Extract actual value from execution state
  \STATE Extract expected value from test assertion
  \STATE Append \texttt{[ASSERT] actual=... expected=... match=T/F} to $V$
\ENDFOR
\STATE \textbf{// Component 3: Loop compression}
\FOR{each consecutive repeated line sequence $S$ in $T$}
  \IF{$|S| \geq 2$ iterations of same loop body}
    \STATE Replace $S$ with single iteration + \texttt{[repeated $\times$N]}
  \ENDIF
\ENDFOR
\STATE Append compressed non-exception lines to $V$
\RETURN $V$
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\section{Tokenizer and Truncation Analysis}
\label{sec:tokenizer_analysis}

DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure driven by tokenizer-induced truncation.
Re-evaluation of the seed 42 checkpoint with the standard max\_length=2048 yields 16\% accuracy, confirming complete model collapse rather than marginal degradation.
The previously reported 84.45\% was obtained with max\_length=16384, which partially bypasses tokenizer truncation.
Seeds 123 and 456, evaluated under identical conditions, achieve 99.16\% and 99.33\% respectively.
The DeepSeek tokenizer averages 2{,}626 tokens per VOTA sample versus 1{,}929 for Qwen, causing 91.7\% of DeepSeek VOTA training samples to exceed the 2{,}048-token context window.
The training framework preserves the verdict label but truncates trace content, so the model trains with incomplete diagnostic information for the majority of samples.
Seeds 123 and 456 (99.16\% and 99.33\%) demonstrate that DeepSeek can learn VOTA when LoRA initialization avoids the truncation-sensitive basin; the 2-seed mean (99.25\%$\pm$0.12) matches the cross-model VOTA range (98.74--99.54\%).

A post-hoc group analysis on seed 42 provides directional evidence: partitioning test samples by whether their training-set counterparts exceeded the context window, intact samples ($N{=}99$) achieve 100\% accuracy while truncated samples ($N{=}1{,}091$) achieve 83.04\% (95\% CI [80.75\%, 85.24\%]; Fisher exact $p{<}.001$), with all 185 errors concentrated in the fail class (fail recall = 31.23\%).
Per-class analysis (Table~\ref{tab:per_class}) confirms that seed 42 achieves 100\% fail precision but only 45.43\% fail recall, systematically defaulting to \texttt{pass}.

Seed robustness is consistent across models: Qwen \texttt{exception\_only} produces identical 99.83\% across all three seeds ($\sigma{=}0$), and DeepSeek achieves 99.39\%$\pm$0.10 (seeds 42/456: 99.33\%, seed 123: 99.50\%).
Because \texttt{exception\_only} test inputs contain 48.99\% duplicates (607 unique of 1,190; \S\ref{sec:dataset}), CIs assume $n{=}1{,}190$ independent trials; under deduplication ($n{=}607$), Qwen's accuracy is 99.67\% (Wilson CI [98.81, 99.91]).

%% ============================================================
\section{Persistent Error Analysis}
\label{sec:irreducible}

The \texttt{exception\_only} condition with Qwen-2.5-Coder-7B misclassifies exactly 2 out of 1,190 test samples across all three seeds (42, 123, 456), with 100\% overlap across seeds.
Both samples (IDs 901 and 905) share the following characteristics:

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Function:} \texttt{check\_dict\_case} (HumanEval/95), a function that checks whether all dictionary keys are uniformly upper-case or lower-case strings.
\item \textbf{Ground-truth label:} \texttt{pass}.
\item \textbf{Predicted label:} \texttt{fail} (false negative).
\item \textbf{Cross-seed consistency:} Both samples are misclassified identically by all three seeds, indicating a systematic rather than stochastic error.
\end{itemize}

Manual inspection reveals the root cause: \texttt{check\_dict\_case} uses \texttt{all()} over a generator expression, and Python's \texttt{all()} short-circuits on the first \texttt{True} value, raising \texttt{GeneratorExit} to terminate the generator.
Because \texttt{GeneratorExit} is a \texttt{BaseException} subclass, the tracer records it as seven \texttt{[ERROR] GeneratorExit} lines, even though the function executes correctly and the test passes.
The model observes these spurious error markers and reasonably but incorrectly predicts \texttt{fail}.
This is not a model failure but a representation ambiguity: the \texttt{exception\_only} format cannot distinguish genuine exceptions from benign \texttt{BaseException} subclasses triggered by Python's iterator protocol.

Most configurations converge to these same 2 errors: Qwen-1.5B, Qwen-7B (3 seeds), CodeLlama-13B (seeds 42/456), and DeepSeek-6.7B (seeds 42/456) all produce error set $\{901, 905\}$.
However, CodeLlama-13B seed 123 achieves 100\% accuracy (0/1190 errors), correctly classifying both samples.
This demonstrates that 99.83\% is a near-perfect \emph{floor} (the convergence attractor for most LoRA initializations) rather than a hard data ceiling: the representation supports perfect accuracy, but most initializations converge to the same 2-error basin.
The practical implication is that these errors are high-probability convergence artifacts addressable through seed selection or ensemble methods, not fundamental limitations of the exception-based representation.

The no-limit condition (81.76\%) recovers and significantly exceeds 1024 tokens ($p{<}.001$), but 1024 tokens is not significantly better than \texttt{no\_trace} (75.13\%; $\Delta{=}{+}2.10$pp, $p{=}.078$, 95\% CI [$-$0.17, $+$4.37]).
This non-monotonicity is specific to head-truncation: the 1024-token prefix retains enough irrelevant content to mislead the model while discarding diagnostic events that appear near the trace terminus.
Under tail-truncation, accuracy increases monotonically for Qwen-7B and Qwen-1.5B (Table~\ref{tab:tail_cross_model}); only DeepSeek-6.7B shows a mild $-$1.5pp decrease at tail-1024$\to$tail-2048, attributable to architecture-specific long-context sensitivity rather than a systematic mid-length pathology.

\paragraph{Comparison to baselines.}
All four trace budget conditions significantly exceed \texttt{no\_trace} except 1024 tokens ($p{=}.078$), confirming that raw trace content provides some signal but unreliably so.
The gap to \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) is massive for every budget condition (18--23pp, all $p{<}.001$), underscoring that even unlimited raw traces cannot substitute for targeted signal extraction.
The best full-trace condition (no\_limit, 81.76\%) still lags \texttt{exception\_only} by 18.07pp (95\% CI [$-$20.34, $-$15.88]).

\paragraph{Interpretation.}
These results rule out input truncation as the primary explanation for the full-trace performance gap: even with unlimited tokens, the model cannot extract the diagnostic signal that VOTA's targeted compression provides.
The non-monotonic dip at 1024 tokens is consistent with a ``worst-of-both-worlds'' regime where the model receives enough noisy context to dilute the signal but not enough to compensate through broader coverage.
The result reinforces the information density interpretation (\S\ref{sec:density}): the gap between full traces and VOTA is driven by the \emph{content} of the trace (irrelevant lines diluting the diagnostic signal), not its \emph{length}.
In contrast, VOTA's compressed representation concentrates the diagnostic signal into fewer tokens, making it sensitive to truncation when those tokens are removed (\S\ref{sec:cross_model}).

\paragraph{Truncation direction.}
Tail-truncation (retaining the last $k$ tokens) dramatically outperforms head-truncation: \texttt{tail\_2048} achieves 97.31\% vs.\ \texttt{head\_2048} (no\_limit) at 81.76\%, a 15.55pp improvement.
Even \texttt{tail\_512} (93.61\%) exceeds every head-truncation condition by over 11pp.

However, \texttt{tail\_256} (77.48\%) performs at the \texttt{no\_trace} baseline level (75.13\%), indicating that the diagnostic signal does not reside in the very last trace lines.
The critical jump occurs between 256 and 512 tail tokens (+16.13pp), localizing the signal window to approximately 256--512 tokens from the trace terminus.
This is consistent with the trace format: the globals module dump consumes the first ${\sim}$384 tail tokens (pure noise), so structured execution markers (\texttt{[Line~X]} variable values) only become visible when the budget exceeds this threshold.

The 18.07pp gap from \texttt{full\_trace} to \texttt{exception\_only} decomposes as: 86\% positional concentration (recovered by tail-truncation at 2048 tokens) and 14\% residual content noise (the 2.52pp gap from \texttt{tail\_2048} to \texttt{exception\_only} that persists regardless of truncation direction).
The fact that \texttt{exception\_only} (99.83\%) still outperforms \texttt{tail\_2048} (97.31\%) confirms that semantic extraction (identifying the exception type and message) is superior to positional extraction (keeping a fixed window), because the model need not filter out non-diagnostic lines that happen to fall within the window.

We analyze the overlap between error sets of different conditions to determine whether they fail on the same samples (Figure~\ref{fig:error_overlap}).

\section{Cross-Model Robustness Analysis}
\label{sec:robustness_analysis}

The cross-model gap pattern (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) suggests a design principle: \emph{trace representations should match the model capability floor, not the ceiling.}
Exception events are consistently the most effective component on both models, and their structural simplicity (a fixed-format error message) ensures that the relative advantage over richer representations holds across all seeds.
All three DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} seeds achieve ${\geq}$99.33\% (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen and CodeLlama at ${\geq}$99.83\%.
VOTA achieves ${\geq}$98.57\% across all models when excluding outlier seeds (cross-model range: 0.80pp), but DeepSeek VOTA exhibits seed-dependent instability: seed 42 (84.45\%) is a training failure due to tokenizer-induced truncation (91.7\% of training samples affected), while seeds 123/456 (99.16\%/99.33\%) match cross-model performance.
This VOTA instability is confounded by tokenizer efficiency and base model differences \citep{yang2024generalization}.
Our \texttt{exception\_only} design sidesteps the truncation confound entirely: inputs have a median of 150 tokens (mean 398), well below the 2{,}048-token context window, so no training samples are truncated on either model.
The resulting 0.50pp cross-model gap (Table~\ref{tab:cross_model}) is therefore a clean measure of model capability differences, making the ``capability floor'' principle directly testable.
The practical implication is that trace-based systems should default to the simplest sufficient signal.

\section{Training Dynamics and Loss Decoupling}
\label{sec:training_dynamics}

The DeepSeek \texttt{exception\_only} results are consistent across all three seeds (99.33/99.50/99.33, $\sigma{=}$0.10pp), matching Qwen's cross-seed stability.
Epoch-level analysis shows mild degradation in seed 42: accuracy peaks at 99.83\% after epoch~1 but settles at 99.33\% by epoch~3 ($-$0.50pp), while seed 456 shows no degradation (99.33\% at both epochs).
Early stopping may yield marginal gains, but the epoch effect is small (${\leq}$0.5pp).
The practical recommendation: for deployment, use task-specific metrics (accuracy, fail recall) for checkpoint and seed selection rather than training loss, and train multiple seeds to select the best.

The contrast with VOTA is instructive: DeepSeek VOTA seed 42 accuracy monotonically increases from 78.15\% to 84.45\% across epochs, consistent with a performance limit from high trace truncation (91.7\% of samples; \S\ref{sec:tokenizer_analysis}).
Seeds 123/456, which avoid the truncation-sensitive initialization basin, achieve 99.16\%/99.33\%, confirming that the deficit is seed-specific rather than a fundamental model limitation.
